title: Smallest Word Using Each Letter Once
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Delete characters from it so that every distinct letter of s is left exactly once. You may only delete; the letters that stay keep their original order.

Of all strings you can get this way, return the one that comes first in dictionary order.

examples.why: "abcd" is not reachable: after the only 'a' there is no 'c' left. Starting with 'b' works, and "bcad" is the smallest way to continue.
The 'x' appears only at the end, so it must be last. Dropping the first 'z' and keeping the second gives "yzx", which beats "zyx".
Only one distinct letter, so one character remains.

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: Build the answer left to right. When is it safe to skip a letter you could place now?
If the letter you just placed is bigger than the next one, and it appears again later, you would rather place it later.
Keep the answer on a stack. For each new letter not already on the stack, pop letters that are bigger than it and still appear later in the string, then push it.

explain.intuition:
You want small letters as early as possible. Suppose the answer so far ends in 'c' and the next letter is 'a'. Putting 'a' before 'c' is better, but only if there is another 'c' later to take its place. If the current 'c' is the last one in the string, you are stuck with it where it is.

That is a monotonic stack. The stack holds the answer built so far. A new letter pops every bigger letter from the top that will appear again later, then goes on top. Letters already on the stack are skipped: their position is as good as it gets, because everything after them on the stack was placed to be as small as possible.
steps: Record the last index of every letter.
Walk the string with a stack and a set of letters on the stack.
If the letter is already on the stack, skip it.
Otherwise, while the top of the stack is bigger than this letter and its last index is after the current one, pop it and remove it from the set.
Push the letter, mark it as used, and at the end join the stack.
pitfalls: Sorting the distinct letters. The result must be a subsequence, and in "dbcadb" nothing can follow the only 'a' except 'd' and 'b'.
Not skipping a letter that is already on the stack. Re-processing it can pop good letters and place a duplicate.
Popping a letter whose last occurrence has already passed. It can never be placed again, so it would vanish from the answer.

complexity.space: O(1) extra, at most 26 letters on the stack

solutions.title: Pick the smallest safe first letter, repeat
solutions.idea: The first letter of the answer is the smallest letter c such that the suffix starting at the first c still contains every needed letter. Fix it, cut the string after it, remove that letter, and repeat.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Build the answer on a stack. A new letter pops bigger letters that appear again later, so small letters move as far left as possible.

followups: Return the smallest subsequence that keeps each distinct letter exactly twice (where the letter appears at least twice). What changes in the pop rule?
Return the largest result in dictionary order instead. Which comparison flips?
